Our assumption posits that a set of LWE (Learning With Errors) samples is indistinguishable from random given a short Gaussian matrix which is carefully chosen to satisfy the required functionality while avoiding problematic leakage.
We provide a thorough cryptanalysis of our assumption, using the extensive cryptanalytic effort against the related evasive LWE assumption (Wee, Eurocrypt 2022 and Tsabary, Crypto 2022) to gain confidence. We emphasize that our assumption is superficially similar but fundamentally different from evasive LWE. Thus, we obtain $\mathcal{iO}$ from a simple lattice assumption whose hardness is somewhat better understood as compared to brand new assumptions.

item.title: New IND-CPA-D Attacks on BFV and BGV
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2546
Authors: Hyeongmin CHOE, Minsik Kang, Damien Stehlé
Summary: IND-CPA-D security is an extension of IND-CPA security introduced in the context of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE). It captures the situation where the computation result is known to the adversary; it is in particular necessary for FHE with threshold decryption. This work presents three new attacks in this situation on the BFV and BGV FHE schemes, when their parameters are instantiated with heuristic assumptions commonly used to enable correctness.
We first extend the \emph{bootstrapping failure attacks} from Cheon \emph{et al.} [CCS'24] on the DM/CGGI and CKKS schemes, to both BFV and BGV. We focus on BGV when instantiated with the so-called powerful-basis representation of ring elements. The second attack relies on \emph{skewing the ciphertext noise} in BFV, making it outpace the heuristic noise bounds for plaintext-ciphertext multiplications. This is achieved by crafting plaintexts, for which the noise bounds do not hold. The third and last attack focuses on outpacing the noise growth in BFV ciphertext-ciphertext multiplications. For this purpose, we \emph{skew the mask} part of the ciphertext by selecting a random encryption of zero, whose addition yields a ciphertext with a sufficiently large mask norm. While the first two attacks successfully recover the secret key, the last attack instead breaks the IND-CPA-D indistinguishability game.
We report experiments on all these attacks, based on the HElib and OpenFHE libraries, respectively, for BGV and BFV. Notably, the second attack implemented in OpenFHE fully recovers the secret key in a few minutes to a few hours, depending on the parameters.

item.title: A Note on the Security of ECDSA with Presignatures or Biased Nonces
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2545
Authors: Geoffroy Couteau, Nikolaos Makriyannis
Summary: Over the years, several ECDSA security experiments have been proposed to enable faster distributed ECDSA signing. These experiments are not known to reduce to the standard ECDSA game, and recent work (Groth and Shoup, Eurocrypt 2022) shows that some are vulnerable, especially when combined with raw signing (signing hash digests directly, rather than pre-hashed messages) and additive key derivation. Furthermore, several of these variants are implemented in public libraries and used by companies, sometimes in commercially deployed products, yet lack sound security foundations.
In this note, we revisit the security landscape of these alternative modes of operation for ECDSA. As our main result, we show that the security of some of these variants, which are used in the wild, is equivalent in the generic group and random oracle model to a standard conjecture from fine-grained complexity on the average-case hardness of the $k$-SUM problem. We complement our study by proving lower bounds, conditioned on fine-grained complexity conjectures, on the running time of generic group model attacks against other standard modes of operation analyzed in (Groth and Shoup, Eurocrypt 2022). Overall, our results provide a complete picture of the security landscape of ECDSA variants, and reveal an elegant connection with (old and new) conjectures from the field of fine-grained complexity.

item.title: Blind-DLPA: An End-to-End Framework for Profiled Blind Side-Channel Analysis
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2544
Authors: Pei Cao, Chi Zhang, Dawu Gu
Summary: Conventional profiled side-channel analysis generally assumes that the plaintexts or ciphertexts associated with target traces are available during key recovery. We consider a profiled blind setting in which the attacker can obtain labeled traces from a profiling device using known inputs and keys, but observes only leakage traces from the target device. Under this setting, we propose Blind-DLPA, an end-to-end multi-task framework for {profiled blind side-channel analysis (profiled BSCA) that processes complete preprocessed trace windows} and jointly estimates the soft Hamming-weight posteriors of an input variable and a key-dependent intermediate variable. These posteriors are combined with pre-computed theoretical joint distributions to rank the key hypotheses, avoiding both manual {point of interest} (PoI) selection and a parameter-sensitive Gaussian label-error model. Evaluations on unprotected AES and Kyber demonstrate successful key recovery, while experiments on protected AES implementations show robustness to desynchronization and Boolean masking. To the best of our knowledge, Blind-DLPA provides the first reported profiled blind key recovery on the ASCAD dataset, reaching a guessing entropy of zero with 39 attack traces. Complementing these results, we revisit the Ascon Hamming-weight joint-distribution model adopted in prior work and identify previously overlooked collisions between key-dependent theoretical distributions that prevent unique key recovery under this model.

item.title: A Key-Recovery Attack on the GTLN Knapsack Cryptosystem via Continued Fractions
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2543
Authors: Shiyi zhou, Yingpu Deng, Shi Ying
Summary: We present a continued-fraction key-recovery attack on the knapsack-based public-key cryptosystem proposed by Gómez-Torrecillas, Lobillo, and Navarro (GTLN). The key observation is that ratios of public-key differences closely approximate rational numbers with small denominators, enabling their exact recovery by continued fractions. Divisibility relations in the recovered fractions yield multiples of two private-key integers through greatest common divisor computations. Once these two integers are identified by a bounded cofactor search, all remaining private-key integers except the modulus and the shift are uniquely determined. Further greatest common divisor computations, cofactor enumeration, and modular inversion then recover the secret modulus and shift. The above process of key recovery uses only public keys. For fixed cofactor bounds, the algorithm runs in polynomial time in the public-key bit length, while a heuristic analysis predicts a high probability of recovering the original key. In experiments with prime-based key generation, our Python implementation recovered the complete private key in all 2,400 trials across the 24 recommended parameter sets, with each attack taking less than 0.05 seconds.

item.title: From if to Oops: Turning a conditional into a key-recovery oracle
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2542
Authors: Gustavo Banegas, Nia Dimitrova, Monika Trimoska
Summary: Deterministic variants of CSIDH remove randomness from the group action, either through implementation techniques or, as in Houben's deterministic CSIDH and OSIDH-LD, by design. Since earlier fault attacks on CSIDH mostly target random point sampling, determinism seems to close that avenue. We show that it opens another: every secret-dependent step occurs at a fixed, public point of every execution, so an attacker can fault the same step repeatedly. Our attack forces the mask that selects which of two lanes computes the next isogeny to zero, for example by skipping one instruction. Whether the output changes reveals whether a secret exponent reaches a chosen threshold, and a binary search over these thresholds recovers the full key with one fault per execution: at most 297 oracle queries for OSIDH-LD and 222 for deterministic CSIDH with CSIDH-512-sized keys. We recover full OSIDH-LD keys in a software fault simulation of the reference implementation, and show on a ChipWhisperer-Lite that the targeted instruction is skipped with probability at least $0.94$ at an isolated fault position. Finally, we argue that fault resistance requires giving up determinism, and propose countermeasures relying on randomization.

item.title: Provable Lattice Reduction in Nearly the Time of QR Factorization
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2541
Authors: Yang Zhou, Zhedong Wang, Mingsheng Wang
Summary: We propose a deterministic lattice-reduction algorithm with bit complexity matching QR factorization up to logarithmic factors, and an implementation that uses fewer instructions than \texttt{flatter} (CRYPTO 2023) in our benchmarks. The key technical innovations are iterative precision management, a finer-grained potential analysis, and a new representation for bases and transformations, all integrated into a recursive framework. We analyze the asymptotic behavior of our algorithm, and show that, for fixed reduction and output accuracy, the running time is $\widetilde O\!\left( n^\omega\bigl(1+\log\kappa_{\rm col}(\mathbf B)\bigr)\right)$, where $\mathbf B\in\mathbb Z^{n\times n}$ is a nonsingular lattice basis and $\kappa_{\rm col}$ is the optimally column-scaled spectral condition number. This gives a finer complexity than prior art, by allowing a tighter condition number $\kappa_{\rm col}$. Besides, through a new observation on the recursive structure, we demonstrate that the algorithm is free from heuristic assumptions. We compare our implementation with \texttt{flatter} on q-ary, NTRU-like, scaled q-ary, and Coppersmith inputs. Our implementation uses fewer instructions in all 153 executions. The median ratios of \texttt{flatter}'s instruction count to ours are 1.55 for ordinary q-ary inputs and 1.86 for NTRU-like inputs.

item.title: Efficient and Compact High-order Masking Raccoon on Memory Constrained Devices
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2540
Authors: Junhao Huang, Yiteng Sun, Jipeng Zhang, Weijia Wang, Donglong Chen, Haiyang Xue, Guomin Yang
Summary: Raccoon, presented at CRYPTO 2024, is a provably secure lattice-based signature scheme featuring an $O(d \log{d})$ masking overhead. Although it did not advance beyond the first-round of NIST's additional call for post-quantum digital signatures, Raccoon remains a promising candidate due to its low masking overhead and strong provable side-channel resistance.
This paper proposes the first efficient and compact implementation of high-order Raccoon on the ARM Cortex-M4, with a focus on optimizing its polynomial multiplication, sampling, and memory consumption. 1) For polynomial multiplication, we present a consecutive 32-bit NTT/INTT implementation for the two moduli in Raccoon, enabling optimal 3+3+3 layer merging to reduce memory-access overhead, together with extensive lazy reduction to minimize modular reductions. As a side contribution, we propose a novel negative double Montgomery reduction technique to accelerate double modular reductions in multi-moduli NTT. 2) For polynomial sampling, we identify and resolve a previously overlooked performance bottleneck caused by frequent incremental SHAKE256 invocations for small data chunks on ARM Cortex-M4. By transitioning to the one-shot approach, we achieve speedups of at least $1.80\times$ across all sampling routines in Raccoon. 3) Finally, we explore memory-saving techniques to enable the practical deployment of high-order masked Raccoon (up to 32 orders) on resource-constrained IoT devices.
The proposed implementations outperform the Raccoon reference implementation by $1.85\times$-$2.25\times$. Notably, high-order masked Raccoon-192 outperforms masked Dilithium3 by $3.12\times, 8.07\times$, and $2.71\times$ at masking orders $d=2$, $4$, and $8$, respectively. Finally, the leakage evaluations confirm that the second-order Raccoon implementation provides strong resistance to differential power analysis (DPA) once micro-architectural transitional leakages are mitigated.

item.title: Implementing Predicate Encryption for Branching Programs: Private Computation over Key-Homomorphic Encodings Without FHE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2539
Authors: Sora Suegami
Summary: Predicate encryption (PE) encrypts a message under an attribute that the ciphertext hides, allowing a secret key for a predicate to recover the message only when the attribute satisfies the predicate. Existing public-key implementations support useful specialized predicates, but enforcing heterogeneous conditions with one key requires an attribute representation fixed before encryption, which grows with the supported types of conditions and cannot express types it does not anticipate, such as regular expressions. Lattice-based PE for general circuits is far more expressive, but existing constructions rely on fully homomorphic encryption (FHE), typically evaluated as a Boolean circuit over key-homomorphic encodings, which expands the computation and amplifies noise growth and leads to impractically large parameters. Existing PE thus offers either practicality for restricted predicates or expressiveness at an impractical cost.
We present a lattice-based PE scheme for branching programs that avoids FHE entirely and combines heterogeneous conditions in a single predicate over a common attribute representation. It rests on two techniques: asymmetric multiplication, which multiplies a hidden program state by an encrypted attribute symbol through decryption inside an encoding, and lookup tables over exponents, which evaluate arbitrary state transitions on a single encoding by ring automorphisms. Under circular Ring-LWE, the scheme is selectively weakly attribute-hiding against polynomially many colluding unauthorized keys.
We give, to our knowledge, the first implementation of PE for a predicate class as expressive as branching programs. On a single NVIDIA A100 GPU, for a predicate that combines a range check and a regular-expression check on a $10$-bit attribute, with parameters targeting $128$-bit security against known Ring-LWE attacks, encryption takes $4.06$ hours, key generation $4.70$ hours, and decryption $4.23$ hours, with $342.25$ GB ciphertexts. These costs remain large, but compared with a single FHE multiplication evaluated as a Boolean circuit over encodings, the basic step of PE that evaluates FHE over encodings, whose ciphertexts alone occupy tens of exabytes per attribute bit, our ciphertexts are at least $2\times10^9$ times smaller per attribute bit, and our decryption needs at least $2\times10^{16}$ times fewer $64$-bit integer multiplications.

item.title: Optimizing HQC with Enhanced Parallel Binary Polynomial Multiplication on GPUs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2538
Authors: DongCheon Kim, JunHyeok Choi, Wai Kong Lee, Seog Chung Seo
Summary: Graphics processing units (GPUs) are widely employed as accelerators in modern servers to handle key-establishment requests in bulk. Such deployments require the GPU implementation to sustain high throughput while keeping each request within its latency bound. In this work, we present a high-performance, end-to-end GPU implementation of Hamming Quasi-Cyclic (HQC), a code-based key encapsulation mechanism (KEM). We propose two novel techniques to accelerate the dominant cost of HQC, which is binary polynomial multiplication over Galois Field GF(2). The first is a parallelization of the Frobenius additive fast Fourier transform (FAFFT), and the second is a mapping of the cyclic product, viewed as a Toeplitz matrix–vector product, onto one-bit integer (INT1) tensor cores. We further explore the design space of these multipliers, measuring them directly on the GPU to derive the best combination for the architecture. We further propose a GPU-resident computation strategy that keeps the entire KEM on the GPU, thereby reducing costly memory traffic. Beyond multiplication, we introduce warp-level parallelization strategies to accelerate the remaining stages, hashing, Reed–Muller/Reed–Solomon (RM/RS) coding, and fixed-weight sampling, which become the performance bottleneck once multiplication is optimized. By varying the mapping of KEM instances to GPU threads, we derive five variants spanning the trade-off between throughput and latency and organize them into a thread-to-KEM mapping taxonomy. On an RTX 4090, the Coarse-Grained (CG) variant maximizes batch throughput. Our multiplier reaches 3,828k polymul/s for standalone multiplication, about 2.9× the latest GPU HQC implementation HIGH, and for the full KEM the CG variant achieves 1.56×, 1.55×, and 2.03× higher end-to-end throughput than HIGH for keygen, encaps, and decaps. For single-shot latency the tensor-core-based BMMAw variant achieves a latency as low as 254 µs. The proposed warp-parallel FGmw variant still attains a latency of 354 µs, demonstrating that our approach remains effective on GPU architectures lacking INT1 tensor-core support. All five variants are further evaluated on an RTX 3090 and an embedded Jetson AGX Orin to confirm cross-platform portability.

item.title: SAT and Neural Network Filters for Misinjections in Fault Attacks
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2537
Authors: Hanbeom Shin, Dongwoo Kang, Donggeun Kwon, Seokhie Hong, HeeSeok Kim
Summary: A misinjection, an injection that misses the fault form an attack assumes, can make an elimination fault attack discard the correct key. They occur when the attacker has not determined the timing of the device, and a random-delay countermeasure wider than the S-box layer can force them even on one who has. This paper presents a SAT filter that removes misinjections without the secret key, one injection at a time. It models the differential propagation from the injected round to the end of the cipher in SAT and rejects an injection when the model has no solution for the assumed fault and the observed ciphertext difference. The paper also presents a neural network filter, which passes an injection when the score of a network trained for the same decision is at least 0.5, and a combined filter, which passes it only when the SAT model of the injection also has a solution. We measure the filters on faults injected by clock glitching into GIFT-64, GIFT-128 and BAKSHEESH on a microcontroller, in three settings, a non-profiling attacker without and with a random-delay countermeasure and a profiling attacker with it. The SAT filter rejected none of the 14669 intended faults and, for the non-profiling attacker without the random-delay countermeasure, at least 0.940 of the misinjections at the full-diffusion round, over at least 385 each. For the same attacker it raises the success probability of ToFA on BAKSHEESH, which recovers the master key, from 5.2% to 61.2%, and the combined filter raises it to 96.2%, each over 2000 trials.

item.title: IISFA: Ineffective Instruction-Skip Fault Attacks on Bitslice Implementations
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2536
Authors: Hanbeom Shin, Dongwoo Kang, Donggeun Kwon, Seokhie Hong, HeeSeok Kim
Summary: Redundancy countermeasures prevent differential fault analysis by withholding faulty ciphertexts. Ineffective fault analysis and statistical ineffective fault attacks exploit executions in which an injected fault leaves the result unchanged, using constraints on intermediate values or statistical bias to recover keys. In this paper, we present an Ineffective Instruction-Skip Fault Attack (IISFA) on bitsliced implementations protected by redundancy. A bitsliced instruction processes $m$ S-boxes simultaneously. Skipping it leaves the group unchanged exactly when all $m$ S-box inputs belong to its ineffective set, which we compute from the implementation. Each ciphertext output by the device therefore restricts all $m$ $n$-bit subkeys to candidates whose S-box inputs belong to that set. The ineffective probability specifies how often a uniformly random S-box input makes the skip ineffective, and its $m$-th power gives the ciphertext output probability for independent inputs. We determine which key candidates remain indistinguishable under a single target instruction. We give key-recovery procedures for both known and chosen plaintexts and combine different target instructions across queries, with one instruction skipped per execution. We calculate expected injection counts or enclosing intervals for the known- and chosen-plaintext procedures from the ineffective sets and use them to reduce the search for efficient target sequences. We evaluate five bitsliced implementations of GIFT, SKINNY and PIPO on an 8-bit AVR microcontroller under a redundancy countermeasure using clock glitches. All measured key-recovery campaigns succeed in every trial.

item.title: Quantum State Search with Classical Interactive Advice
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2535
Authors: MOHAMMED BARHOUSH
Summary: We study whether a quantum verifier can find a hidden quantum state by exchanging classical messages with an unbounded prover who knows the state. The verifier has access to a reflection oracle about the target. For a Haar-random $n$-qubit target, we prove that achieving constant average fidelity with the target requires $(q+1)^2(B+1)=\Omega(2^n)$, where $q$ is the number of verifier queries and $B$ is the total prover-to-verifier communication. The bound allows arbitrary classical interaction and unrestricted computation between queries. Our proof extends the lower bound of Aaronson and Kuperberg from a single classical proof to an arbitrary classical interaction.
As a result, we obtain a quantum-oracle separation of UniqueQMA from QCIP with polynomially many classical messages. In particular, we give a unitary oracle $\mathcal{U}$ such that there exists a language $L\in\mathrm{UniqueQMA}^{\mathcal{U}}$ but $L\notin\mathrm{QCIP}^{\mathcal{U}}$.
We further give an oracle construction for a notion known as QMA-QCIP[2] gap problem. This gives average case hardness for a QMA language under classical access to a QCIP[2] decision oracle and is used in establishing negative results on witness encryption and quantum indistinguishability obfuscation.

item.title: Circular Dragon: $\widetilde{{O}}$ptimal Adaptively Secure Distributed Randomness/Key Generation and Parallel Broadcast
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2534
Authors: Hanwen Feng, Yuan Lu, Tiancheng Mai, Qiang Tang
Summary: We present the first strongly adaptive common coin protocol, under the PKI setup (in the random oracle model and the algebraic group model, yet with no trusted dealer), that (i) achieves the optimal resilience $t< n/2$ in synchronous networks, and (ii) attains near-optimal asymptotics: near-quadratic communication $O(\kappa \lambda n^2\log n)$ and logarithmic rounds $O(\kappa\log n)$, with failure probability $\textsf{negl}(\lambda)+2^{-\kappa}$, where $\lambda$ (resp. $\kappa$) is the computational (resp. statistical) security parameter. Furthermore, the coin protocol assumes no memory erasure. At its core is a ``special-purpose'' distributed key generation (DKG) protocol that produces a secret in an elliptic-curve group. Our common coin immediately implies the first strongly adaptive and optimally resilient Byzantine Agreement with subcubic communication and sublinear rounds in the absence of a trusted dealer. Furthermore, we give two non-trivial applications of independent interest: (i) a strongly adaptive Parallel Broadcast (PBC) under standard PKI with near-quadratic communication and logarithmic rounds, whereas all existing subcubic solutions (Gelles et al. CRYPTO'25, Civit et al. PODC'24) require at least linear rounds; (ii) a strongly adaptive ``general-purpose'' DKG for field-element secrets with $O(\lambda\kappa n^2\log n)$ communication and $O(\kappa\log n)$ rounds (assuming memory erasures), fully compatible with legacy threshold schemes (BLS, Schnorr, ElGamal), improving upon (Feng et al. PODC'24), which requires $O(\lambda\kappa n^{2.5} \log n)$ communication and $O(n)$ rounds. Our core is a new design methodology, which we call \emph{Circular Dragon}. This extends the Dragon method (PODC'24) that was originally developed for sub-cubic communication DKG protocols but with linear rounds, by further reducing the round complexity.

item.title: Off-Key: Inconsistent MAC Keys Compromise Privacy in SPDZ-Family MPC
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2533
Authors: Marcel Keller, Sela Navot, Nirvan Tyagi
Summary: SPDZ-family protocols for maliciously secure multi-party computation protect secret-shared values with message authentication codes (MACs) under a secret-shared global key. Their security requires that all values and preprocessing used together be authenticated under the same key. We present Off-Key, a privacy attack that exploits violations of this requirement. Depending on which specific MAC check protocol is used, a corrupted party can either recover the value of a shared secret from a single authentication check or test a guess through selective failure by modifying a MAC share and observing whether a masked check succeeds. While this attack does not compromise the theoretical security guarantees of the protocols, we demonstrate this key-consistency vulnerability in evaluated versions of MP-SPDZ, SCALE-MAMBA, and FANNG-MPC, which allow a corrupted party to use different keys across batches, threads, or process runs. To help implementations avoid this class of attacks, we identify the state that enforces key consistency in representative preprocessing protocols and show how preserving and reusing it prevents the attack.

item.title: HERMES: High-Performance Private Decoding for Large Language Models
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2532
Authors: MohammadHossein Olyaiy, Cora Shao, Dingqing Yang, Mohammad Shahrad, Mieszko Lis
Summary: Privacy-preserving inference (PI) enables users to query large language models (LLMs) without revealing their prompts, but incurs substantial computation and communication overhead. Prior PI systems primarily optimize prefill and time to first token (TTFT). This suits applications that need only a single output token, yet most real-world use cases require multi-token responses. Such autoregressive workloads are dominated by time per output token (TPOT) instead.
For the first time, we investigate generating full multi-token answers for real prompts under PI. We show that PI decode is hindered by two bottlenecks: (i) nonlinear kernels that require many interactive communication rounds, and (ii) attention protocols that underutilize ciphertext capacity and repeatedly re-encrypt or transmit the growing key and value (KV) cache.
We present HERMES, a PI system optimized for LLM decoding. HERMES replaces high-round nonlinear protocols with compute- and bandwidth-intensive alternatives that require fewer communication rounds. It also introduces a novel matrix-multiplication protocol based on homomorphic encryption that keeps the KV cache encrypted on the server and uses grouped-query attention (GQA) to improve ciphertext utilization. On Llama 3.1 8B Instruct, across the network conditions and prompts used in our evaluation, HERMES lowers TPOT by up to 2.7× and total PI latency by up to 2.1×.

item.title: High-Precision CKKS with Focal Units
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2531
Authors: Jung Hee Cheon, Junho Lee
Summary: In CKKS, higher precision requires a larger scaling factor, increasing modulus consumption during homomorphic arithmetic and leaving less modulus available after bootstrapping under the same modulus budget. We introduce Focused CKKS, which trades unused SIMD slots for precision through focused rescaling and key-switching based on cyclotomic units. These units reduce error in selected focus slots while allowing larger error in the background slots. Using only a $1/k$ fraction of the slots provides approximately $k$ times as many bits of precision at the same scaling factor and CKKS parameter setting. Such a high-precision multiplication costs the same as an ordinary CKKS multiplication, with each focus slot supported by $(k-1)$ background slots. More generally, the construction supports different precision requirements across slots.
We also construct a bootstrapping procedure tailored to Focused CKKS. Only the base modulus at the bottom level needs to grow with the target precision; the remaining bootstrapping computation maintains approximately the same modulus consumption by using fewer slots. By adapting the high-precision bootstrapping based on discrete CKKS and performing its error-cleaning step in Focused CKKS, we further reduce this base modulus by approximately the same factor $k$.

item.title: Computing endomorphisms of superspecial principally polarized abelian surfaces in time and memory \(p^{4/5+o(1)}\)
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2530
Authors: Marc Houben, Lam L. Pham
Summary: We present an algorithm for computing endomorphisms of superspecial principally polarized abelian surfaces over finite fields. Under a standard heuristic, we obtain a non-scalar polarized endomorphism in expected time and memory $p^{4/5 + o(1)}$.

item.title: The Covering Radius of $\text{RM}(1,9)$ is Precisely $242$
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2529
Authors: Xiang-dong Hou, Evelyn Sabo, Freeman Slaughter
Summary: Let $\text{RM}(r,n)$ be the $r$th order Reed-Muller code of length $2^n$, and let $\rho(r,n)$ denote its covering radius, so that $\rho(1,n)$ is the largest possible nonlinearity of a Boolean function in $n$ variables. For odd $n$, the value of $\rho(1,n)$ was previously known only for $n\le 7$. It is known that $242\le\rho(1,9)\le 244$, but the exact determination of $\rho(1,9)$ has been a long-standing open question. We give a computer-assisted proof that $\rho(1,9)=242$. We first show that a function of nonlinearity $243$ would yield one of nonlinearity $244$, so it suffices to exclude $244$. Divisibility properties of the Walsh spectrum then attach to any function of nonlinearity $244$ a cubic $p$ whose spectrum attains the sharp bound $\sum\limits_a|W_p(a)|\le 10240$, and the cases of equality take one of two forms. One form is eliminated directly. The other is eliminated by an exhaustive computation that leverages the classification of the $349$ orbits in $\text{RM}(3,9)/\text{RM}(2,9)$ under $\text{GL}(9,2)$, using Langevin's catalog of representatives together with an audit of its completeness, and the enumeration is carried out twice with independent implementations. The notebook to verify the computer search portion, $\texttt{Verify_RM(1,9).ipynb}$, contains all data and recomputes each check, and may be found in the repository $\texttt{https://github.com/FreemanSlaughter/Covering-Radius}$.

item.title: Revisiting the Security of VDOO
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2528
Authors: Siyu Li, Hao Guo, Peigen Li, Siyong Tao
Summary: VDOO is a multivariate signature scheme submitted to the Next-generation Commercial Cryptographic Algorithms Program (NGCC). We study the security of its submitted parameter sets. In this paper, VDOO is described as a multilayer Rainbow construction. By retaining only its last oil space, we obtain a generalized UOV instance and apply existing wedge attacks.
For the parameter set targeting 512-bit security, we estimate costs of $2^{432}$ and $2^{379}$ gates for the reconciliation and intersection variants, respectively. These estimates rely on the assumptions of the attack model and are below both the claimed security level and the attack costs reported in the specification.
Our analysis uses only the generalized UOV structure. The additional information in the multilayer structure may allow further improvements. Our results also motivate further study of parameter choices that balance resistance to known attacks with signing efficiency.

item.title: How Secure are NTRU+ Keys? Analysing the Best Module Attacks
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2527
Authors: Paola de Perthuis, Filip Trenkić
Summary: A recent analysis of module-BKZ [Ducas–Engleberts–Perthuis, Asiacrypt'25] predicts subexponential speedups for lattice reduction on module lattices over cyclotomic fields whose conductor has small odd prime factors. This threatens NTRU+, the South Korean standard for key encapsulation, and related schemes; however, the short vectors one seeks to find are short in the coefficient geometry, whereas module-BKZ operates in the canonical geometry.
We introduce relative canonical and relative coefficient embeddings, realising a module over a cyclotomic field $K$ as a module over any subfield $L$, and characterise when the two agree up to scaling: exactly when the radicals of their respective conductors $c$ and $\ell$ satisfy $\mathrm{rad}(c)/\mathrm{rad}(\ell) \in \{1,2\}$. Furthermore we quantify the distortion incurred in general when passing between embeddings, and hence identify the optimal subfield for module-BKZ and BKZ to use.
Estimating the cost of the best attack with simulation-based models [Perthuis–Trenkić, PQCrypto'26], we find that the best module attack saves only 4–10 blocksizes, costing NTRU+ keys at most three bits of security in the Core-SVP model.
We further extend the analysis of overstretched NTRU regimes [Ducas–Woerden, Asiacrypt'19] to the module setting, and find the fatigue point is reached sooner than with unstructured counterparts, though NTRU+ parameterisations remain safe.

item.title: Faster ABE for Turing Machines from Circular Evasive LWE
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2526
Authors: Valerio Cini, Hoeteck Wee
Summary: We present a new ABE for Turing machines, where
- encryption runs in time $O(T)$ and produces a ciphertext of size $O(T)$ for time $T$ computation; - key generation produces a key of size $O(1)$; - security relies on the (public-coin) circular evasive LWE assumption.
In fact, we obtain an ABE for a simple and more general model of computation which we refer to as iterated (local) computation. We improve on the recent construction of Agrawal, Kumari, and Yamada (CRYPTO 24) in three ways: (i) faster encryption and smaller ciphertext size; (ii) smaller key size, and (iii) weaker assumptions, eliminating the need for circular tensor LWE.

item.title: Enjoy FAEST on Hardware: Efficient and Novel Hardware Acceleration of Emerging Post-Quantum Digital Signature Scheme FAEST
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2525
Authors: Brendan Funk, Jiafeng Xie
Summary: The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) standardization process has drawn significant attention from the research community recently, especially regarding these PQC schemes' hardware acceleration. Nevertheless, related research on the emerging schemes, e.g., those currently under consideration by the NIST additional digital signature scheme standardization, still needs further exploration. With this background, this paper presents an efficient and novel hardware acceleration for FAEST, one of the promising signatures in the NIST Round 3 additional scheme competition. Overall, we have presented several layers of innovative efforts to obtain the proposed acceleration. First of all, we have conducted detailed algorithmic analysis on the major computationally intensive operations within FAEST and proposed novel design strategies and algorithms for their efficient hardware implementation. Next, we have proposed novel design efforts to construct these major operations into efficient building blocks to finalize the overall accelerator, along with the help of optimized operational phase workflow. The dedicated extension to build the L1-EM-fast accelerator is also given. Finally, we have provided a detailed and thorough evaluation process to showcase the superior performance of the proposed design over the existing complete, Sign part, and single security level MPC-in-the-head signature acceleration works. For instance, at the same security level, the proposed fast variant has at least 98\% less equivalent Area-Delay Product (eADP) than the recent complete SDitH design. To the authors' best knowledge, this is the first hardware acceleration work for FAEST, and we hope the outcome of this research will facilitate the ongoing PQC standardization process.

item.title: Homomorphic Encryption for High-precision Arithmetic of Approximate Numbers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2524
Authors: Shihe Ma, Jiaming Liu, Anyu Wang, Xiaoyun Wang
Summary: The CKKS fully homomorphic encryption scheme enables efficient arithmetic over complex numbers, but each homomorphic multiplication consumes a large modulus to ensure enough precision, limiting both the circuit depth and precision supported by CKKS. This work addresses this problem by proposing Generalized CKKS (GCKKS), a CKKS analogue of the GBFV scheme (EUROCRYPT 2025) that trades the number of slots for reduced modulus consumption.
Despite its high-level similarity to GBFV, GCKKS faces new challenges caused by the different encoding and encryption structures of CKKS. We address these challenges with novel techniques not present in GBFV. Our plaintext encoding starts with an improved and SIMD version of Costache, Smart, and Vivek's encoding in 2017. Namely, it rounds complex values to cyclotomic integers instead of Gaussian integers, and reduces the rounding problem to solving CVP instances. This encoding allows storing high-precision complex values in polynomials with small canonical norms. As an important observation, the encoding can be simplified to a sparse CKKS encoding followed by multiplication with a polynomial constructed from a short vector in the encoding lattice. We show that by integrating this encoding format into GCKKS decryption, most GCKKS homomorphic operations and the corresponding noise analyses reduce to their CKKS counterparts. This relieves GCKKS from any heavy computational or noise overhead.
In experiments, GCKKS provides 7 levels with 1000-bit precision at ring dimension $2^{14}$, where each multiplication takes less than 30 ms. To our knowledge, this precision has never been achieved before. It can be used to preserve enough precision after noise flooding, a necessary ingredient for CKKS circuit privacy and a common approach to secure threshold CKKS and to provide IND-CPA$^\text{D}$ security.

item.title: GKS Fully Homomorphic Encryption: Security Analysis
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2523
Authors: John Graham, Soundes Marzougui, Milos Pavlovic, Vladimir Shpilrain
Summary: All traditional encryption schemes share a fundamental operational vulnerability: encrypted data must be decrypted before it can be used. Fully homomorphic encryption eliminates this vulnerability by enabling computation directly on encrypted data, but existing FHE schemes impose substantial practical constraints that limit deployment. This paper presents a formal security analysis of the Gribov-Kahrobaei-Shpilrain (GKS) private-key FHE scheme. GKS requires no bootstrapping or de-linearization, produces bit-exact decryption, supports native encrypted search, and scales to unbounded depth.

item.title: Superspecial points on Humbert surfaces and the probability of (N,N)-splitting
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2522
Authors: Tanush Shaska
Summary: Let $p\equiv3\pmod4$ be a prime and let $N\geq2$ be an integer. We determine, to first order in $1/p$ and with an explicit error bound, the proportion of superspecial principally polarized abelian surfaces over $\overline{\mathbb{F}}_p$ that are optimally $(N,N)$-split. The surfaces are weighted by the reciprocals of their automorphism orders, which is the stationary measure of the Richelot random walk. The main theorem states that for $p\nmid N$ the expected number of optimal $(N,N)$-splittings of a surface is exactly $5NJ_2(N)(p-1)/(p^2+1)$, where $J_2$ is Jordan's totient; that for $p>2N^2$ the second factorial moment is $c_N/(p^2+1)$ with $c_N$ independent of $p$; and consequently that, for fixed $N$, the proportion of split surfaces is $5NJ_2(N)/p+O_N(p^{-2})$. The constants $c_N$ are determined explicitly for $2\leq N\leq7$. This proportion is the stationary target density of the splitting-detection attack on the superspecial isogeny problem in dimension two. It was previously known only from experiments or from a one-sided bound. The method is to show that the superspecial surfaces sample the genus of their refined Humbert invariants with Siegel's weights, which makes Siegel's theorem on genus averages available. The same method gives the first moment of primitive representations of every discriminant prime to $p$, mixed moments for several levels, an exact probability at level $2$, and a proof that the geometric upper bound of earlier work has the correct leading term. All results are proved; the enumerations enter only through the values of $c_N$, and every formula was additionally confirmed by exact computation at twelve primes.

item.title: Eﬃcient Fixed-Point Implementation of Mitaka
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2521
Authors: Shiduo Zhang, Paul Kirchner, Xiuhan Lin, Yang Yu
Summary: The Mitaka signature scheme is a variant of Falcon (FN-DSA). It has a considerably simpler signing procedure that can be parallelized while retaining Falcon's efficiency advantage. Mitaka offers two different signing approaches: a default one relying on floating-point arithmetic and an alternative, called MitakaZ, avoiding floating-point arithmetic at the cost of more Gaussian samples. Despite its better portability, MitakaZ has not previously been implemented in practice.
This work presents an efficient fixed-point implementation of the Mitaka signing algorithm. We optimize the MitakaZ Gaussian sampler to make it suited to fixed-point arithmetic while achieving higher efficiency. Specifically, we replace the wide integral Gram root decomposition used in MitakaZ with a fixed-point square Cholesky decomposition, which substantially reduces the cost of integer Gaussian sampling. We prove bounds on intermediate values and representation errors without empirical assumptions on their magnitudes. The distributional analysis models each integer Gaussian call as exact at its represented inputs. We provide a fixed-point implementation of the new Mitaka signing algorithm in C. On an Intel Core~i7-1360P, our native AVX2 implementation generates signatures in an average of 361 kcycles for Mitaka-512 and 707 kcycles for Mitaka-1024, measured with Linux hardware performance events. On an ARM Cortex-M4F STM32F411, the corresponding measured costs are 4.0 and 7.8 Mcycles.

item.title: GPU Acceleration for Boyar-Peralta Algorithm in High Dimensional Linear Layers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2520
Authors: Xiao Huang, Chao Sun, Ge Wu, Liquan Chen
Summary: The design of lightweight cryptographic schemes necessitates efficient circuit implementations of linear layers. A commonly used metric for evaluating circuit efficiency is the number of XOR gates required. For a given linear transformation over $\mathbb F_2$, finding its circuit implementation with the minimum number of XOR gates is referred to as the Shortest Linear Program (SLP) problem. As a prominent heuristic, the Boyar-Peralta (BP) algorithm provides competitive results, and numerous subsequent studies have introduced further optimizations. However, the inefficient implementations of the BP-like algorithms significantly limit their applicability to high-dimensional and dense matrices, and effective solutions to these performance bottlenecks remain scarce.
In this paper, we address the performance bottlenecks of the BP algorithm and its variants (e.g., A1, A2 and BP-LSL) both theoretically and practically. We introduce the meet-in-the-middle (MITM) approach to reduce their theoretical time complexity. Practically, we re-design the implementation framework of these algorithms to fully leverage GPU parallelism, which significantly reduces the time spent on computing multiple XOR sums of bases, performing binary search, and updating distances. Meanwhile, we also propose a candidate pruning mechanism to reduce the computational burden on the GPU side and further improve the overall efficiency. Compared with the original implementations, we significantly accelerate the solving process for both normal and depth-constrained scenarios while maintaining the same solution quality.
Our experimental results demonstrate that, for a 26-dimensional matrix with density 0.5, our implementation requires only 9.44 seconds on an entry-level GTX 1650 GPU, achieving a speedup of over $6{,}200\times$ compared with the current recursive, exhaustive, and one-threaded implementation. Using a high-performance RTX 4090 GPU, we extend the solvable boundary to 64-dimensional sparse matrices and 42-dimensional matrices with density 0.381. For 32-dimensional dense matrices, our accelerated A1 algorithm successfully establishes some new g-XOR records, including a 172-step g-XOR implementation for Whirlwind M0 and a 170-step implementation for Whirlwind M1. Besides, we also provide a 157-step g-XOR sequence for AES-InvMixColumn matrix with depth 5 through our BP-LSL implementation. Based on our accelerated BP implementation, we construct some MDS matrices with dimension 40 or more. For $4\times 4$ blockwise circulant matrices of dimensions 40, 48, and 64, the minimum g-XOR sequence lengths we found are 110, 132, and 184.

item.title: DPA-style Attacks on VOLE-in-the-Head Signature Schemes
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2519
Authors: Jinnuo Li, Shu Han, Yunyan Zou, Fan Zhang, Puwen Wei, Weijia Wang, Hao Cheng
Summary: VOLE-in-the-Head (VOLEitH) has emerged as a promising paradigm for the design of post-quantum signatures, as it enables efficient signing and verification while also achieving small signature sizes. In the ongoing NIST PQC standardization process for additional digital signatures, two VOLEitH signature schemes, namely FAEST and SDitH, have advanced to the third round. Regarding their practical security, especially resistance to power side-channel attacks, existing studies have focused on only a few specific operations, and thus a comprehensive analysis remains lacking. To address this gap, we present, to the best of our knowledge, the first DPA-style attack framework against VOLEitH signatures. Our framework targets the secret witness, whose recovery permits the generation of valid signatures for arbitrary messages. Based on this framework, we systematically analyze the leakage stemming from the computation of sensitive intermediate values involved in VOLE correlations, and characterize how such leakage can be linked to secret witness hypotheses for mounting DPA-style attacks. As a consequence, we propose six classes of DPA-style attacks on FAEST and SDitH, including two vertical and four horizontal attacks. Finally, the proposed attacks are validated using both simulated leakage under varying noise conditions and practical measurements on three ARM Cortex-M4 devices, demonstrating their effectiveness in both settings.

item.title: Associated-Data Correlations in Eevee: Deterministic Forgeries against Nonce-Misuse Security
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2518
Authors: Takanori Isobe, Mostafizar Rahman
Summary: Eevee's Umbreon and Espeon modes claim online authenticated-encryption security under nonce reuse. We give an independent analysis of associated-data correlations that yield probability-one non-empty-message forgeries with three encryption queries and one verification query. Two AD-only tags reveal a mask difference that translates a ciphertext to another AD value. The basic attacks and their proof diagnosis overlap with independent and concurrent work by Mao et al. Our complementary contribution is a systematic affine treatment of partial final message blocks. For any admissible fixed final-fragment length r, n-r+3 encryption queries suffice; allowing the forged length to be r or r-h for a chosen 1 <= h < r < n, while choosing the source plaintext adaptively, reduces this to n-r+2. Both constructions satisfy the padding check and succeed with probability one. They apply to general message lengths, with at least one preceding complete block for Espeon. We also analyze the published short-message Espeon AD omission, validate the published complete-block Umbreon attack using the official ForkSkinny primitive in a specification adapter, and report a separate two-query attack accepted by the unmodified public C modes. Finalization is discussed only as an unproved countermeasure direction.

item.title: Zippel: A Language, Compiler, Runtime, and Analyzer for ZK Proof Systems
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2517
Authors: Sebastian Angel, Sydnie-Shea Cohen, Eleftherios Ioannidis, Pratyush Mishra, Alex Ozdemir, Yuxiang Qiu, Alireza Shirzad
Summary: This paper introduces Zippel, a language, compiler, runtime, and analyzer for cryptographic proof systems. Zippel lets developers write proof systems with ease using syntax that mimics pseudocode in cryptography papers. It also eliminates entire classes of vulnerabilities by construction owing to its type system and runtime. For example, Zippel automatically synchronizes protocol transcripts and correctly applies the Fiat--Shamir transform. Zippel also has fully automated static analyses that confirm whether a protocol is complete and sound given only the protocol's description. We have implemented 35 proof systems in Zippel including Sumcheck, Schnorr, KZG, Groth16, Bulletproofs, Hyrax, Spartan, Dory, HyperPlonk, DeKART, and Pari. Our evaluation shows that Zippel programs are competitive with hand-written implementations on multi-core hardware, so Zippel's security and implementation benefits do not come at high cost.

item.title: Watermarking Proofs with Provenance-Binding ZK-SNARKs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2516
Authors: Wenhao Wang, Fan Zhang, Charalampos Papamanthou
Summary: The emerging ecosystem of outsourced proving services, decentralized prover networks, and prover marketplaces raises a new requirement for ZK-SNARKs: the need to watermark proofs with provenance information, such as the prover identity and a fresh request-time nonce. The prover identity records who should receive credit for the proof, while the nonce binds the proof to a particular request and is intended to prevent the prover from reusing work performed before that request was created. The key security requirement is that a prover must perform fresh work—comparable to computing the proof from scratch—when generating a proof for a fresh provenance, even if the attacker may have generated the same proofs before or performed precomputation.
Prior attempts, such as Succinct Network, proposed embedding provenance information in the Fiat-Shamir challenges, though without a rigorous security definition or analysis. We show that this approach is not secure and is vulnerable to preprocessing attacks, in which an adversary can precompute provenance-independent information that can later be used to reduce the effort required to generate proofs for a fresh provenance. We instantiate these attacks against KZG-PLONK.
To arrive at a secure construction, we propose the first formal definition for provenance-binding ZK-SNARKs to capture the above desired property. We present a generic construction that augments code-based polynomial commitments, such as BaseFold and FRI, with provenance binding. Compiling them with Poly-IOPs yields provenance-binding ZK-SNARKs. Our construction incurs minimal overhead.

item.title: CHAMP: Cayley HAshing with Matrix Products
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2515
Authors: Alexander Demin, Alexey Ovchinnikov, Vladimir Shpilrain
Summary: Cayley hash functions hash binary strings by representing the bits of the message as elements of a semigroup and multiplying the corresponding elements. This gives Cayley hash functions useful homomorphic properties. Here, we propose CHAMP, a Cayley hash function based on products of $2\times 2$ matrices over a finite field, and discuss its security, implementation, and performance.

item.title: Analysis of the Multi-Key Optimization for SPECK
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2514
Authors: Marco Baldi, Michele Battagliola, Rahmi El Mechri, Paolo Santini, Riccardo Schiavoni
Summary: SPECK has recently been introduced as a code-based digital signature scheme exploiting the similarities between the Permuted Kernel Problem (PKP) and the Permutation Code Equivalence Problem (PEP). By utilizing PEP as a trapdoor for PKP, SPECK achieves a significant speedup compared to LESS, replacing expensive Gaussian elimination with vector-matrix multiplications. This comes at the cost of larger signatures, since each round of the Zero Knowledge (ZK) protocol used in SPECK has soundness error $1/2$.
A well known technique to reduce the soundness errors (and thus the number of parallel repetitions and, ultimately, the signature size) in ZK proofs based on group actions consists in giving multiple elements in the public keys. Despite being constructed around an instance of PEP, which admits a natural description as a code-based group action, the protocol employed in SPECK deviates from the traditional proof of knowledge used for group actions. As shown by the authors of SPECK, a naive use of the multi-key optimization may lead to concrete security concerns. Therefore, the question on whether such a technique can be applied successfully to SPECK remains open.
In this paper, we give a positive answer to such a question. We revisit the multi-key optimization for SPECK and investigate the underlying security concerns in detail, identifying conditions and parameter constraints under which multiple keys can be securely integrated into the protocol. Even though, when instantiated with conservative parameters, the multi-key optimization leads to unappealing performance, we show there is wide room for improvements. Furthermore, we design a ring signature scheme based on the same underlying construction.

item.title: Fully Homomorphic Encryption for Small Batches of Complex Numbers
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2513
Authors: Jules Dumezy
Summary: We propose a new approximate homomorphic encryption scheme to process small batches of complex numbers. Leveled operations are based on a new shaped rounding, whose error is a multiple of a fixed public ring element $g$, small on the data slots and larger on the others. The unused slots form a guard band that is computed on but never decoded, and the polynomial scaling factor $g^{-1}\Delta$ generalizes the CKKS scaling factor, with $g=1$ recovering CKKS. Guard-domain bounds determine the scaling factor needed for stability, while a norm bound limits the precision gain for a given guard amplification. A replicated layout uses a unit from a small cyclotomic subring to preserve shaping under admissible rotations and traces. We give a native bootstrapping algorithm whose forward transform reads only data slots, and conversions to and from CKKS with shared keys. Security reduces to Ring-LWE with the same parameters as CKKS. In poulpy, at ring degree $2^{15}$ and parameters targeting 128-bit security, bootstrapping a ciphertext holding 16 or 64 values restores 21 levels and retains at least 22.6 bits of minimum precision after 21 sequential products by fresh operands, while sparse CKKS supports only four levels at that degree and comparable precision. For these batch sizes, bootstrapping to restore 16 levels is about 5 times faster on one thread than sparse CKKS, which requires ring degree $2^{16}$.

item.title: SLEEK: Sparse Quasi-Cyclic Codes with Closed-Form DFR Key Encapsulation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2512
Authors: Alessandro Annechini, Alessandro Barenghi, Marco Gianvecchio, Gerardo Pelosi
Summary: Performance in terms of bandwidth and execution time, as well as decoding failures remain important challenges for code-based KEMs. This paper introduces SLEEK: Sparse quasi-cycLic codEs with closEd-form DFR Key encapsulation, a Key Encapsulation Mechanism (KEM) based on Quasi-Cyclic Moderate-Density Parity-Check (QC-MDPC) codes. The scheme employs a parallel bit-flipping decoder with three iterations and a closed-form estimate of the decoding-failure rate (DFR). The latter allows parameter selection with analytically bounded failure probability and supports the use of standard IND-CCA transformations. We designed two variants of SLEEK. The first, SLEEK-LT, targets IND-CCA security for long-term keys, and supports QC-MDPC codes with different rates, allowing a tradeoff between public-key and ciphertext size. The second, SLEEK-E, targets IND-CPA security for ephemeral keys in settings requiring forward secrecy. While SLEEK-LT makes conservative choices and aims at security against active attackers, SLEEK-E relies on a novel QC key structure, for which we establish security equivalent to that of the original QC-MDPC construction under the same assumptions, while reducing key-generation cost. We explore a broad design space and provide parameter sets targeting $128$-, $192$-, and $256$-bit security, together with an $80$-bit configuration for constrained embedded platforms. We also optimize polynomial inversion and parallel bit-flipping decoding, the two dominant components of the implementation. We provide quantitative benchmarks of our optimized AVX2 implementation of SLEEK. For SLEEK-LT, ciphertexts are $4.9\times$ smaller than those of the NIST standard choice, HQC, at the cost of a $47$% increase in the runtime, and is $1.3\times$ to $2.7\times$ faster than BIKE. For SLEEK-E, execution time improves by $1.6\times$ over HQC with a bandwidth usage reduced by $2.1\times$. Compared with Lean-BIKE, SLEEK-E is $5.3\times$ faster and substantially reduces the impact of decoding failures on system reliability.

item.title: I Want to Ride My BIKE: Customizing Bit-Flipping Decoders for Ephemeral Key KEMs
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2511
Authors: Davide De Zuane, Marco Gianvecchio, Alessandro Annechini, Paolo Santini, Marco Baldi, Alessandro Barenghi, Gerardo Pelosi
Summary: Large public keys and ciphertexts remain a major obstacle to the deployment of post-quantum cryptosystems in applications currently relying on compact classical schemes. In code-based post-quantum key encapsulation mechanisms, reducing the Decoding Failure Rate (DFR) generally requires larger parameters, further increasing communication and storage overheads. Ephemeral key-pair scenarios allow a different trade-off: ideally, each secret key is used for a single decapsulation, limiting the opportunities to observe and exploit decryption failures. We investigate how this setting can be used to reduce the public-key and ciphertext sizes of code-based key encapsulation mechanisms such as BIKE. We present the first optimized implementation of the $\textsf{BF-max}$ decoder: compared with conventional parallel bit-flipping decoders currently used by BIKE, $\textsf{BF-max}$ provides better error-correction capability, but its computational structure makes an efficient implementation less straightforward. Combining $\textsf{BF-max}$ with other decoders from the literature, we introduce decoding strategies that offer different trade-offs among DFR, execution time, public-key size, and ciphertext size.
Experimental results show that the proposed design reduces both public-key and ciphertext sizes by 7.8\% compared with LeanBIKE, a BIKE variant specifically designed for ephemeral-key use, while retaining similar execution time and DFR. For additional context, the selected parameter set yields a combined public-key and ciphertext size that is 22\% smaller than that of BIKE and smaller by a factor of 2.79 than that of HQC. Note that BIKE and HQC, unlike LeanBIKE and our design, target the long-term-key setting. As a concrete application, we show that the solutions we propose make it possible to incorporate BIKE into constrained protocols, such as Internet Key Exchange version 2 (IKEv2), in which no code-based KEM would otherwise fit.

item.title: Secure Compilation of Probabilistic Side-Channel Countermeasures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2510
Authors: Gilles Barthe, Gaëtan Cassiers, Henri Dohmen, Marc Gourjon, Benjamin Grégoire, Nora Khayata, Thomas Schneider, Finn Schubert
Summary: Probabilistic countermeasures are a common means of protecting programs against side-channels. These countermeasures are hard to implement and are routinely broken by compilers. Proving that a compiler preserves probabilistic side-channel security directly would require reasoning about perfect simulatability of distributions, a challenging technique normally reserved for high-assurance cryptography in frameworks like EasyCrypt and out of scope for compiler correctness.
In this paper, we present a language- and leakage-model-agnostic framework for provably secure compilation of probabilistic side-channel security notions. Our main contribution is formalizing a deterministic leakage-preservation relation that implies preservation of probabilistic security notions, including d-NI and d-SNI for masking and cryptographic constant-time. Our framework establishes the same guarantees without probabilistic proof obligations, reducing preservation to a per-pass simulation argument on deterministic traces.
We use the Rocq proof assistant to prove that a model of the core pipeline and several optimizing passes of the Jasmin compiler preserve security in the value-probing model with glitches. We also show how to harden against transition leakage with lightweight annotations at the source level. On top of this, we build libmasking, an open-source library of arbitrary-order masked gadgets in Jasmin that securely compiles to ARM and RISC-V assembly, provides C language bindings, and is benchmarked on real hardware. Together, these contributions are a step towards programming environments in which masked code is written or generated, verified at the source level, optimized, and compiled without breaking security.

item.title: Sparse Secrets, Dense Problems: Efficiently Masking HQC in Hardware
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2509
Authors: Fabian Buschkowski, Niklas Höher, Tim Güneysu
Summary: HQC has recently been selected by NIST as a code-based alternative to ML-KEM and is currently undergoing standardization. While multiple timing and power side-channel attacks against HQC have been presented, application of masking has so far only been studied for software implementations.
As part of this work, we close this gap by first proposing a novel masking technique for the sparse-dense vector multiplication, one of the core components in all HQC operations. We manage to securely exploit the sparsity of the secret operand using a mixed Boolean and arithmetic masking technique and prove its first-order security in the transition- and glitch-robust probing model as well as its PINI-composability. With the same memory width, our configurable and highly parallelizable masked design takes only 3% more clock cycles than a previous unprotected HQC multiplier. Furthermore, our technique requires only 81 bits of randomness per cycle, irrespective of its parallelism. However, like previous Rotate-and-Add constructions, it is vulnerable to profiled horizontal side-channel attacks, which recover all support indices within ±8 positions from 200 traces of our FPGA implementation despite TVLA showing no signs of leakage after 10 million traces. To prevent such attacks, we integrate efficient hiding countermeasures natively into the architecture of the multiplier, resulting in only 1.7% additional latency and moderate area overhead.
Together with efficiently masked fixed-weight samplers and a masked decoder, we present the, to our knowledge, first fully masked hardware implementation of HQC, supporting first-order masked key generation, encapsulation, and decapsulation. Notably, our masked key generation is faster than a previous unprotected design from literature on an Artix-7 FPGA. Lastly, all modules of our complete designs show no signs of first-order leakage after 1 million traces.

item.title: Power Analysis on SQIsign via Ideal Reconstruction from Quaternion Leakages
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2508
Authors: Won Kim, Jaeho Jeon, JeongHwan Lee, Suseong Lee, Young-Sik Kim, Changmin Lee
Summary: SQIsign is an isogeny-based signature scheme, which is one of the Round-3 candidates for NIST's additional post-quantum digital signature standardization. NIST considers resistance to side-channel attacks as one important factor in evaluating digital signature schemes. However, side-channel analysis of SQIsign remains very limited. To the best of our knowledge, all existing studies target the Round-1 version, so their applicability to the substantially revised Round-3 SQIsign has not been established. Moreover, existing studies either provide experimental validation only for toy parameters or assume exploitable leakage without demonstrating its extraction in practice, leaving their applicability to realistic implementations unclear.
In this work, we identify five side-channel vulnerabilities in the signing procedure of Round-3 SQIsign and provide polynomial-time algebraic algorithms that recover the secret key from the corresponding leaked intermediate values. Additionally, we further provide algorithms that enable the reconstruction of the complete secret key even when the side-channel leakage reveals only partial bits of an algebraic value, for each vulnerability. Finally, we further perform power analysis attack on the SQIsign source code, extracting the necessary leakage or its partial information for each vulnerability.

item.title: safeRNSgcd: Accelerating Falcon key generation with RNS in SafeGCD
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2507
Authors: Cesare Huang, Bo-Yin Yang
Summary: The deepest level of Falcon's NTRU solver needs only one Bézout coefficient from two large integer resultants already represented in a residue number system (RNS). We give $\mathtt{safeRNSgcd}$, which computes this coefficient while keeping the large states in RNS. Its central insight is that centered explicit CRT can recover the exact low bits needed by SafeGCD batches using single-word fixed-point arithmetic. Integrated into $\mathtt{ntrugen}$, our C implementation reduces inversion and private-key basis-generation costs on a Raspberry Pi 5 and two x86-64 processors, compared with original $\mathtt{ntrugen}$ and a variant omitting the unused coefficient.

item.title: Efficient Two-Dimensional Representation Evaluation via Dual Isogenies with Applications to Isogeny-Based Cryptography
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2506
Authors: Jianming Lin, Saiyu Wang, Chang-An Zhao, Yuhao Zheng
Summary: The evaluation of two-dimensional isogeny representations is a fundamental operation in many isogeny-based cryptographic schemes, notably the public-key encryption schemes POK\'{E} (Eurocrypt 2025) and PIKE (PKC 2026), as well as the digital signature schemes SQIsign2D-West (Asiacrypt 2024) and SQIsign2DPush (Eurocrypt 2026). However, existing two-dimensional evaluation algorithms rely on time-consuming discrete logarithm computations and torsion-basis generation, creating a severe performance bottleneck for the entire protocol. In this paper, we propose a novel algorithm for evaluating two-dimensional representations by leveraging the properties of dual isogenies, thereby eliminating the need for costly discrete logarithms. We apply this methodology to significantly accelerate some isogeny-based protocols, including POK\'{E}, SQIsign2D, and their variants. We provide optimized C implementations for the speed-optimized variants of POK\'{E} and SQIsign2D using our proposed method. Experimental benchmarks demonstrate that the fast variants of POK\'{E} combined with our new techniques achieve computational speedups of up to $3.47\times$ in terms of CPU clock cycles compared to POK\'{E} at the NIST-I security level. Additionally, our explicit analysis and implementation results confirm that the signing phase of SQIsign2DPush (resp. the NIST post-quantum cryptography standardization candidate SQIsign-v3.0), when using our method, achieves a performance improvement of up to $11.24\%$ (resp. $5.02$\%) across the three NIST security levels.

item.title: AVX-512 Acceleration of SQIsign 3.0 Verification
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2505
Authors: Yunqi Wen, Xuzhe Liu, Zhi Hu, Saiyu Wang, Chang-An Zhao
Summary: SQIsign is a compact isogeny-based signature scheme. We present a low-latency AVX-512 implementation of complete SQIsign 3.0 verification at security levels I, III, and V. Our implementation provides vectorized curve-side verification, including the Superglue transition, and introduces dynamic-programming strategies for the degree-$2^\ell$ and theta-model $(2,2)$-isogeny chains. The strategies account for batched point evaluation and the preparation of SIMD data. On an Intel Core i7-11800H running native Ubuntu 24.04, the complete verifiers achieve $2.14\times$, $2.08\times$, and $2.34\times$ speedups, respectively, over the SQIsign 3.0 Broadwell reference verifiers (the optimized 64-bit assembly implementation).

item.title: Byzantine Broadcast in $\widetilde{O}(n^2)$ Communication
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2504
Authors: Yuval Efron, Jovan Komatovic, Ling ren
Summary: We present a deterministic $n$-party Byzantine broadcast protocol secure against $t<n$ faults, with communication complexity $O(n^2\log^4(n)\lambda)$ and $O(t)$ rounds (where $\lambda$ is a security parameter), improving upon the seminal Dolev--Strong protocol from 1983.

item.title: SwiftAuth: Conditional Privacy-Preserving UAV Authentication with Multi-Source Credential Aggregation and Non-Interactive Authorization
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2503
Authors: Mingwei Zeng, Qingyang Zhang, Jie Cui, Hong Zhong, Fengqun Wang
Summary: To address the challenges of interactive credential issuance and conditional privacy-preserving authentication for dynamic terminals accessing multiple third-party services, we propose an traceable and aggregatable tagged witness signature (TA-TWS). Building upon this scheme, we design an efficient and privacy-preserving anonymous authentication framework, termed SwiftAuth. SwiftAuth decouples the issuer’s authorization phase from the user’s credential acquisition process in traditional anonymous authentication systems by introducing an asynchronous credential distribution mechanism. This allows issuers to generate authorization components even when users are offline, while ensuring that only the designated user can derive the complete access credential. Furthermore, during the authentication phase, SwiftAuth reduces communication and verification overhead in concurrent multi-service access by compressing multiple credentials into a constant-size representation, and supports verifier-side batch verification across users. In addition, it provides conditional privacy by integrating a regulatory trapdoor, ensuring default anonymity for legitimate users while enabling authorities to trace malicious actors upon protocol violations. Finally, we formally prove that the proposed TA-TWS achieves unforgeability and witness hiding. Extensive experiments were conducted on multiple resource-constrained devices, and Aliyun servers, using the MIRACL Core cryptographic library, demonstrate the practicality and efficiency of our approach.

item.title: Shorter Hash-Based Signatures via Guarded Sharing in a DAG Model
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2502
Authors: Chongxu Ren, Hongbo Yu
Summary: Stateless hash-based signatures are among the most important post-quantum signature schemes. Although they have been standardized by NIST, they still have large signatures. Within these constructions, the few-time signature component is receiving increasing attention. Recent work has introduced new techniques, including rejection sampling, forced pruning, bucket thinning, and hash chains.
In this work, we continue to improve few-time signatures with a new technique, guarded sharing. Our construction moves beyond the previous tree-based model to a DAG-based signature. By combining guarded sharing with bucket thinning, hash chains, and rejection sampling, we obtain a new signature scheme called BGS-CC.
Our construction further improves on the state-of-the-art few-time signature BPORS-C+BFP. Most notably, for 128-bit security and a small use quota of $Q=2^{24}$, it yields complete signatures of 2,228 bytes. To our knowledge, this is the first SPHINCS-based stateless signature to be shorter than the 2,420-byte signatures of the standardized module-lattice scheme ML-DSA-44.

item.title: Aerie: Efficient Aggregation of Falcon Signatures
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2501
Authors: Alberto Centelles, Quang Dao, Mohammadtaghi Badakhshan, Justin Thaler
Summary: The post-quantum signatures selected by NIST are ten to over a hundred times larger than the elliptic-curve signatures they replace. Moreover, unlike the BLS signatures that blockchains use to aggregate validator votes, they do not aggregate natively. Both problems can be addressed with a SNARK: a short proof that a batch of signatures is valid, replacing the signatures themselves.
The prevailing approach, central to Ethereum's roadmap, pairs hash-based signatures with hash-based SNARKs. This is slow because the prover must prove many hash evaluations per signature. We instead aggregate lattice-based signatures with a lattice-based SNARK.
We present Aerie, a proof system for aggregating Falcon-512 and Falcon-1024 signatures. By retaining each signature's short random salt in the aggregate, Aerie lets the verifier compute the hashes directly. The proof then covers only algebraic and norm checks. Aerie combines protocols tailored to these checks with the Akita polynomial commitment scheme. Unlike prior Falcon aggregation schemes, it also proves that the signatures satisfy Falcon's byte-format requirements.
On an Apple M4 Max laptop without GPU acceleration, Aerie aggregates 32,768 Falcon-512 signatures, roughly the number of validator votes in one Ethereum slot, in 0.65 seconds. A single proof covers the whole batch, with no recursion. The aggregate is 42.1 bytes per signature including the salts, or about 66 KiB in total if the signatures share one salt. It verifies in 54 milliseconds on one core, 10× faster than checking the signatures individually. On one core, proving takes only about 8× as long as individual verification. We prove knowledge soundness of Aerie in the classical random-oracle model and derive aggregate unforgeability from Falcon's security.

item.title: GhostFaceMPC: Privacy-Preserving Face Recognition with Multi-Party Computation
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2499
Authors: Davide Carnemolla, Dario Catalano, Mario Di Raimondo
Summary: Facial recognition has become central to modern authentication systems, security frameworks, and personalized services. However, its widespread adoption is hindered by severe privacy risks, particularly surrounding unauthorized access to sensitive biometric data. To address these challenges, this paper presents GhostFaceMPC, the first end-to-end, privacy-preserving face recognition system to evaluate a deep convolutional neural network extractor and matching under secure multi-party computation. GhostFaceMPC enables secure processing of facial data across all stages of a face recognition process, from feature extraction and storage to matching, without exposing raw images or biometric embeddings at any stage. We introduce a multi-party computation-friendly quantization of the GhostFaceNet model and circuit optimizations that make face recognition under multi-party computation practical. The code is available at https://github.com/crypto-unict/GhostFaceMPC.

item.title: Noise-Tolerant Quantum One-Time Programs Using Stateless Trusted Hardware, Revisited
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2498
Authors: Prabhanjan Ananth, Divyanshu Bhardwaj
Summary: A quantum one-time program scheme is a functionality-preserving compiler that transforms a program into a quantum state that can be used to obtain only one output of the program. Our goal is to design quantum one-time programs that can be realized on existing quantum technologies. Our contributions are two-fold:
1. We design a BB84 state-based quantum one-time program scheme in the stateless trusted hardware model that is resilient to single-qubit corruption errors and detectable erasure errors. To illustrate, under independent noise with a 90% detectable erasure rate and a 3% Pauli Y-error rate on surviving qubits, a signature token of 39,801 BB84 qubits achieves forging probability at most $\small 2^{-128}$ against at most $\small 2^{32}$ classical verification queries, with honest failure probability below $\small 10^{-6}$. Prior to our work, [Behera, Sattath, and Shinar TQC'22] studied a BB84 state-based quantum one-time program scheme resilient to independent single-qubit corruption errors; our construction treats detectable erasures separately.
2. We give two extensions to our scheme. First, we study the setting wherein the same trusted hardware can be reused across different independently generated quantum one-time programs. Second, we study the setting wherein multiple trusted hardware devices are used and the security holds as long as at least one of them is not compromised.

item.title: SecAgg++: A Post-Quantum Privacy Preserving Federated Learning Protocol
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2497
Authors: Alessandro Perez, Giulia Cavicchioni, Silvio Cretti, Riccardo Longo, Alessandro Tomasi, Silvio Ranise
Summary: Secure aggregation is a fundamental building block for privacy-preserving federated learning, yet most existing masking-based secure aggregation protocols do not provide post-quantum security. In this work, we present SecAgg++, a masking-based post-quantum secure aggregation protocol for the single-server setting. SecAgg++ integrates post-quantum cryptographic primitives while preserving the communication and computational efficiency of classical frameworks such as SecAgg and SecAgg+, and supports client dropout handling through an efficient recovery procedure.

item.title: Structural Cryptanalysis of the Eevee AEAD Family
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2496
Authors: Shuping Mao, Peng Wang, Jiadong Han, Tingting Guo, Yan Jia, Ying Chen
Summary: Eevee is a family of three AEAD modes, Umbreon, Jolteon, and Espeon, proposed at CCS 2023 for IoT-to-cloud secure computation. We analyze structural flaws in the algorithms of the supplied full-version specification and the proof steps underlying their online authenticated-encryption claims. An AD-free, two-encryption prefix distinguisher has advantage $1-2^{-n}$ in the ideal-forkcipher model, contradicting the specified online ideal object. Independently, the separable associated-data transform yields a four-encryption nonce-misuse distinguisher with advantage $1-2^{-n}$, a deterministic AD-only forgery, and nonempty-message forgeries obtained from cross-domain state differences. These attacks contradict the advertised nonce-misuse bounds of Umbreon and Espeon. With nonce-respecting encryption queries, one two-block Jolteon encryption permits a fresh one-block forgery with the same tag, while Espeon's short-message path permits arbitrary AD substitution. We trace these counterexamples to failures of online-prefix consistency, conditional transcript distributions, domain separation, and checksum freshness in the original proof. The authenticity attacks follow from deterministic identities, and the privacy counterexamples persist with an ideal forkcipher. We derive corresponding requirements for AD processing and message finalization, and briefly summarize supporting checks of the published C routines.
