The central failures concern the mode design and cannot be resolved solely by correcting implementation encodings.

item.title: Issuer-Independent Decentralized Exchange for E-Cash
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2495
Authors: Roozbeh Sarenche, Omid Mirzamohammadi
Summary: Despite decades of cryptographic advances, electronic cash (e-cash) remains largely confined to payments and lacks the broader decentralized financial applications built around cryptocurrencies. As a step toward broadening its application layer, we present an issuer-independent e-cash exchange in which a liquidity provider holds inventories of two independently issued e-cash currencies and users trade between them without requiring either issuer to participate in individual swaps. Our design combines a blockchain settlement layer, which automates the exchange and makes its execution publicly verifiable, with an exchange-compatible e-cash protocol. Classical e-cash must be adapted to this setting in two respects: payments must become publicly verifiable by the exchange, and the additional privacy risks created by public execution must be addressed. We formalize these new privacy requirements and construct a compact e-cash realization with publicly verifiable payments and aggregate anonymous reissue. We prove the security and privacy properties of the resulting exchange protocol under the stated cryptographic and issuer-functionality assumptions.

item.title: Speeding up Sumcheck using Algebraic Geometry
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2494
Authors: Rahul Dalal, Benedikt Bunz, Tamir Hemo, Ron D. Rothblum
Summary: The sumcheck protocol, a ubiquitous component of modern proof-systems, enables proving the sum of evaluations of a low-degree multivariate polynomial. In theory, sumcheck has been generalized from polynomials to (tensors of) any multiplication code, a code whose pointwise products of codewords lie in a related product code. All practical systems nonetheless specifically use polynomials. For proof-systems over binary fields that target Boolean circuits, this choice has a real cost: the product of two binary messages under Reed--Solomon is no longer binary. As a result, the prover's work in the first, and most expensive, round of sumcheck (the so-called univariate skip) grows by a logarithmic factor.
We present a new concrete multiplication code based on algebraic geometry that is binary-preserving: the product of two encoded binary messages is again a binary message. Specifically, we construct an explicit multiplication code over $\mathbb{F}_{2^{128}}$ that carries $64$-bit messages to binary product messages of length $222$, and whose product code has relative distance greater than $1-2^{-119}$. The part of the product message that the prover actually sends in sumcheck is more than $3 \times$ smaller than with Reed--Solomon, as used in practice. The code comes from a genus-$95$ curve over $\mathbb{F}_2$ with $64$ rational points, built as a $(\mathbb{Z}/2)^3$ Artin--Schreier cover of a genus-$4$ curve.
We implemented the resulting protocol, which we call the AG skip, inside the Flock proof-system. For $2^{32}$ constraints, it speeds up the skip round by $2.36\times$ and the whole zerocheck, which was the prover's most expensive component, by $1.65\times$.

item.title: Robust ECDSA Threshold Signing at Scale
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2493
Authors: Carsten Baum, Anders Dalskov
Summary: This work presents an efficient, scalable, and robust threshold ECDSA signing protocol for the $t\leq (n-1)/3$ scenario, making it suitable for e.g., bridging consensus from one Blockchain to another. Our construction allows to batch-compute pre-processing material for efficient online signing. While our protocol is based on established ideas for (Verifiable) Secret Sharing, we optimize it to scale efficiently both in terms of computation and communication with a large number of signers. We therefore combine efficient batching techniques for sharing (Fitzi & Hirt, PODC 2006), randomness extraction (Beerliova-Trubiniova & Hirt, TCC 2008) and share opening (Damgård & Nielsen, CRYPTO 2007) with recent advances in efficient Zero-Knowledge proofs (Attema & Cramer, CRYPTO 2020). We implement and evaluate the protocol experimentally and show that it is practical for large number of parties $n$.

item.title: Threshold Post-Quantum E-Voting from Lattice Commitments
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2500
Authors: Jalal Alizadeh
Summary: Lattice-based homomorphic e-voting protocols built on commitments, such as EVOLVE, keep ballots private against all but one authority and the tally verifiable even if all authorities collude, but need every authority to tally. We present T-EVOLVE, in which votes are Shamir-shared over the commitment message space: any t of n authorities that took part in the checking phase complete the tally, privacy holds against t-1 colluding authorities and verifiability against all. The voter proves that her committed shares form a Reed-Solomon codeword whose value at zero is a valid vote; the parity checks cost no communication, and tallying interpolates public column sums without norm growth. Complaints of authorities, including about ciphertexts that do not decrypt, are publicly verifiable given encryption with publicly verifiable opening, which we define and instantiate under LWE. We prove privacy, verifiability, individual verifiability and robustness in the classical random oracle model; the verifiability reduction is not tight and the parameters rest on classical hardness estimates. In our C implementation, a yes/no ballot for four authorities takes 109 KB without signatures, or 147 KB with the computed seed ciphertexts of our instantiation, and an authority aggregates 10^4 ballots in about three minutes per successful tally round on one core.

item.title: Exploring Fault Injection Attacks on HQC and BIKE Beyond Fujisaki-Okamoto Verification
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2492
Authors: Thales B. Paiva, Lucas C. Cardoso, Keerthi Kamalakshan, Hariprasad Valsaraj Kelassery, Marcos A. Simplicio Jr., Shivam Bhasin
Summary: Fault injection attacks have been extensively studied in the context of post-quantum cryptography, yet existing analyses on code-based KEMs largely focus on faults targeting the Fujisaki-Okamoto transform. This work presents new fault injection attacks against BIKE and HQC that operate beyond this commonly protected component and target less obvious instructions within the decapsulation process. The proposed attacks achieve full key recovery using only valid ciphertexts under NIST Level 1 parameters, requiring 17392 and approximately 3 million decapsulation queries for HQC and BIKE, respectively. In addition, we introduce a general approach to identify effective fault locations by analyzing decoder behavior under perturbed conditions. The attacks are experimentally validated on an STM32H7 microcontroller using laser fault injection, demonstrating high repeatability. These results reveal a broader attack surface and provide a foundation for more efficient fault attack analyses in future work.

item.title: Shift-Invariant Permutations with Polynomial Composition: Construction and Algebraic Structure
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2491
Authors: Cheng Lyu, Dabin Zheng, Mu Yuan, Lei Hu
Summary: Shift-invariant permutations of \(\mathbb F_2^n\) are particularly attractive in symmetric cryptography because of their regularity and implementation efficiency. Constructing such permutations with an explicit algebraic structure remains a challenging problem. In this paper, we study a family of shift-invariant transformations of \(\mathbb F_2^n\) constructed from a recursively defined sequence of mappings \(\{\gamma_j\}_{j\ge 0}\) associated with landscapes. First, we prove that, under an explicit dimension condition relating \(n\) to the support of the landscape, the sequence \(\{\gamma_j\}_{j\ge 0}\) has the polynomial composition property if and only if the corresponding landscape is quasi-conserved on \(\mathbb F_2^n\) with a nonzero special index. Then, we determine the eventual zero or periodic behavior of \(\{\gamma_j\}_{j\ge0}\), including the exact index at which the sequence either first vanishes or becomes periodic, together with the least eventual period, and establish linear independence until the first linear relation occurs. When the polynomial composition property holds, we establish an explicit isomorphism between the group of permutation elements in the monoid generated by these mappings and the unit group of a quotient ring \(\mathbb F_2[z]/\langle p(z)\rangle\), where \(p(z)\) is a monomial or a binomial determined by the landscape. This framework reduces the tasks of testing bijectivity, computing iterates, and determining compositional inverses and orders of permutation elements to polynomial computations. Finally, we apply the results to mappings represented by binomials and trinomials in the quotient ring, obtaining explicit criteria and formulas, and tabulate more than one hundred representative constructions of shift-invariant permutations, recovering and unifying several previously studied families.

item.title: Reaction Attack on CKKS Deployments with Asymptotically Optimal Query Complexity
item.description:
Paper: 2026/2490
Authors: Song Bian, Hyeongmin Choe, Jiseung Kim, Changmin Lee
Summary: We study a protocol-level reaction leakage in CKKS deployments where public coefficient-to-slot (C2S) evaluation keys are combined with a client's 1-bit validity response. Under this deployment surface, a malicious evaluator can recover a ternary secret key using asymptotically optimal $O(\mathcal{H})$ reaction queries, where $\mathcal{H}$ is the entropy of the secret key.
The attack does not break RLWE or CKKS IND-CPA security. Instead, it exploits the interaction between client-side validity reactions and public homomorphic linear transformations. A shift of a public encryption key yields a ciphertext whose plaintext is a function of the secret key; the public ${\sf C2S}$ layer then repacks this information to construct a ciphertext whose validity depends strictly on whether a targeted secret coefficient matches a guessed value. Furthermore, each submitted query is independently randomized with a fresh encryption of zero, so that each resulting malicious ciphertext appears entirely distinct, thereby allowing the attack to simply evade trivial detection mechanisms on the client side.
We implemented the full end-to-end attack in Lattigo v6.2.0 and recovered the full secret key across four parameter sets drawn from standard CKKS presets. For uniform ternary secrets, the attack uses $O(N)$ queries and is within a factor $2/\log_2 3 < 2$ of the oracle-only entropy lower bound. For sparse ternary secrets, a tailored variant further reduces the number of queries in practice. Our results show that observable validity reactions form a practical key-recovery channel in CKKS deployments exposing this surface, even when the underlying cryptographic assumptions remain intact.
